claim: The paper formulates Cartesian impedance dynamics as an LPV model and embeds a successively linearized Safety Control Barrier Function constraint in a linear MPC, yielding a convex QP that predictively varies impedance to avoid modeled obstacles while minimizing deviation from nominal impedance. Under the equality constraints, model assumptions, and alpha conditions stated in Proposition 3, the error dynamics are globally asymptotically stable; the safety claim is limited to forward invariance of the modeled safe set and does not establish unconditional physical or human safety.
claim_locator: Method sections defining LPV impedance dynamics, predictive impedance variation, and SCBF-constrained MPC; Proposition 3; free-motion and human-guided experiments; discussion.
epistemic_status: author-reported results with conditioned theoretical claims and bounded reader inference
problem_and_setting: Safe physical human–robot collaboration in which a robot should retain nominal Cartesian impedance but temporarily alter it when predicted motion approaches an obstacle, evaluated in free motion and human-guided peg manipulation near fixed obstacles with a Franka Panda.
method_or_mechanism: Cartesian impedance error dynamics are represented as an LPV system. Linear MPC predicts robot motion and linear human guidance; at each step, a linearized SCBF forward-invariance constraint produces a convex QP selecting impedance variation while penalizing deviation from nominal impedance. Nominal translational stiffness is 150 N/m, rotational stiffness 10 N/rad, and damping twice the square root of stiffness.
content_summary: Proposition 3 establishes global asymptotic stability only for specified constrained error dynamics and alpha/model conditions. Franka Panda experiments ran at 1 kHz using CVXGEN on an Intel Xeon E3-1245, with ten-step prediction and control horizons spanning 1 s, Q=I6 and R=0.1I3. In free motion the robot avoided a fixed obstacle at [0.4,0,0.45] m with 0.05 m safety distance and returned toward the nominal path; larger gamma was less conservative. Relative to a nonpredictive method, prediction reduced reported collision-risk duration, improved obstacle bypassing and reduced trajectory error. Human-guided trials showed anticipatory deviation and later recovery. Mean QP solve time was 95.8 microseconds for the evaluated experiment, not a worst-case guarantee.
synthesis_role: Primary evidence for predictive optimization-based variable impedance with explicit safe-set constraints, separating conditional forward-invariance and stability guarantees from broader physical-safety claims.
development_link: Extends nonpredictive impedance-variation obstacle avoidance by adding robot-motion and human-guidance prediction inside an SCBF-constrained MPC.

evidence.finding: Global asymptotic stability is proved for the error dynamics under the paper's equality constraints, model and alpha conditions.
Successive SCBF linearization and linear predictive dynamics form a convex QP for minimally invasive impedance variation.
The controller ran at 1 kHz with ten-step horizons covering 1 s.
The robot avoided the fixed obstacle with 0.05 m safety distance and returned toward nominal motion; increasing gamma reduced conservatism.
Prediction shortened modeled collision-risk duration, improved bypassing and reduced trajectory error.
Impedance changed before modeled collision risk and recovered after risk diminished.
Mean QP solve time was 95.8 microseconds on the stated hardware and trials.

boundary_conditions: Forward invariance applies only to the SCBF-encoded safe set and assumed model.
GAS applies only under Proposition 3 conditions.
Convex optimality depends on linear guidance and linearized dynamics.
Experiments used fixed obstacles and selected trajectories; moving obstacles were not tested.
The 95.8 microsecond value is a mean, not worst-case timing.
Unexpected interactions, collision aftermath and ISO certification were not evaluated.
assumptions: LPV and linearized dynamics approximate the robot over the horizon.
Human guidance is sufficiently represented by the linear predictor.
Obstacle state and safe set are known accurately.
The QP remains feasible and timely.
Discretization and linearization errors stay within the tested regime.

reported: Robot or human-guidance model mismatch can degrade performance.
The predictor cannot anticipate a sudden force increase before interaction and is not uniformly accurate.
Complex industrial and accidental interactions were outside scope.
inferred: The GAS proof does not cover unmodeled dynamics, infeasibility, solver overruns or discretization error.
SCBF geometric invariance does not establish universal injury safety or certification.
Fixed-obstacle tests do not validate moving or uncertain obstacles.
Mean solve time does not establish worst-case schedulability.
